chapter.title: The one equation

cards.body:
Stand on the pavement outside a house on a Tuesday. The house, the car in the drive, the sofa, the 3,000 in the kitchen drawer: that is what the family **owns**. The mortgage and the plumber's unpaid bill: that is what they **owe**. Whatever is left when you take one from the other is theirs.

A balance sheet is that same photo, taken of a company instead of a house.
cards.simpler:
Picture a family's house on an ordinary Tuesday. The house, the car, the sofa and the 3,000 in the kitchen drawer are things the family **owns**. The mortgage and the plumber's unpaid bill are things they owe. Take what they owe away from what they own, and whatever is left belongs to them.

A balance sheet is the same snapshot, but of a company instead of a family.

cards.prompt: Maya's house would sell for 300,000 today. She has 20,000 in the bank. Her mortgage still has 250,000 left on it. If she sold up and paid the bank off tonight, how much walks out the door with her?

whyNot.b: That's everything she owns, not what's left: the bank still has a claim on 250,000 of it.
whyNot.c: That's the mortgage, what she owes the bank, not her share.

cards.reteach: Add up what Maya owns: 300,000 house plus 20,000 cash is 320,000. Take away what she owes: 250,000. The gap, 70,000, is hers. Own minus owe equals yours.

cards.title: Three words, one equation
cards.body:
A balance sheet has three totals and nothing else matters as much. *Assets* are what the company owns: cash, buildings, stock on shelves, money customers still owe it. *Liabilities* are what it owes: bank loans, unpaid supplier bills, tax due. *Equity* is what is left for the owners.

The equation is the house again. **Assets minus liabilities equals equity.** Accountants usually write it the other way round, assets equals liabilities plus equity, but it is the same sentence.

Find those three totals and you have read the skeleton of any balance sheet in the world.
cards.simpler:
A balance sheet comes down to three totals. Assets are what the company owns: cash, buildings, goods on shelves, and money customers still have to pay. Liabilities are what it owes: bank loans, unpaid supplier bills, tax due. Equity is what is left over for the owners.

The rule is the house again. **Assets minus liabilities equals equity.** Accountants often write it as assets equals liabilities plus equity. It is the same sentence either way. Find those three totals and you have read the bones of any balance sheet.

cards.title: Rosa's bakery, one Monday
cards.body:
Rosa's bakery owns an oven worth 12,000, has 4,000 in the till and bank, and 1,000 of flour and butter in the storeroom. Total assets: 17,000. She owes her flour supplier 2,000 and the bank 10,000 on the oven loan. Total liabilities: 12,000.

Equity: 17,000 minus 12,000, so 5,000. If she sold everything at those prices and paid everyone off, she would leave with 5,000 and a very clean kitchen.
cards.simpler:
Rosa runs a bakery. She owns an oven worth 12,000, has 4,000 in the till and bank, and keeps 1,000 of flour and butter in the storeroom. What she owns adds up to 17,000. She owes her flour supplier 2,000 and the bank 10,000 for the oven. What she owes adds up to 12,000.

Take 12,000 from 17,000 and you get 5,000. That is her equity. If she sold everything and paid everyone back, she would walk away with 5,000.

cards.prompt: The bottom of Kite Ltd's balance sheet shows total assets of 900 and total liabilities of 600. What should the owners' share line read?

whyNot.a: That's assets plus liabilities, adding what you own to what you owe. Owing more does not make the owners richer.
whyNot.c: That's the liabilities total, what Kite owes, not what is left after paying it.

cards.reteach: Kite owns 900. Of that, 600 is spoken for by lenders and suppliers. The 300 that nobody else can claim belongs to the owners. That is equity: owns minus owes.

cards.title: Why the two sides always match
cards.body:
Every single asset was paid for by somebody. Either a lender put the money in, which creates a liability, or the owners did, which is equity. So **the two sides match by definition**, not by luck. Equity is simply the gap that makes them equal.

This is why the sheet is called a *balance* sheet. If total assets does not equal total liabilities plus equity, you are looking at a typo, not an insight.

On a real sheet, look for the lines named *Total assets*, *Total liabilities* and *Total equity*. Equity sometimes hides under *shareholders' funds* or *net assets*. Same thing, different hat.
cards.simpler:
Every asset a company has was paid for by someone. Either a lender gave the money, which creates something owed, or the owners put it in, which is equity. So **the two sides match by definition**. It is not luck. Equity is just the gap that makes them equal.

That is why it is called a balance sheet. If assets do not equal liabilities plus equity, someone made a typing error.

On a real sheet, look for the lines called total assets, total liabilities and total equity. Equity sometimes goes by shareholders' funds or net assets. Same thing, different name.

cards.body: Dev opens a supermarket's annual report, sees a line reading *Total liabilities and equity: 2.4 billion*, and tells the group chat the company owes 2.4 billion. It does not. That combined line is always identical to total assets; it is the other side of the photo. How to spot it: if the big number at the bottom of the right side exactly matches the big number at the bottom of the left, it is the sum, and the real debt is a smaller line above it.
cards.simpler: Dev opens a supermarket's annual report. He sees a line that says total liabilities and equity: 2.4 billion. He tells his friends the company owes 2.4 billion. It does not. That line adds together what the company owes and what belongs to the owners, so **it always equals total assets**. It is the other side of the same picture. The real debt is a smaller line higher up. If the big number on the right matches the big number on the left exactly, it is the sum, not the debt.

cards.prompt: A friend says: "This company's balance sheet balances, so it must be in good shape." Which reply is right?

options.text: It always balances, because equity is defined as assets minus liabilities. Balancing says nothing about health.
Right. If assets equal liabilities plus equity, the company can pay its debts.
It only balances in years the company made a profit.

whyNot.b: That's the chapter 6 health check, not the equation: matching sides is bookkeeping, not an ability to pay.
whyNot.c: That's the income statement's job, not the balance sheet's: a profit or loss just changes the size of equity, and the sides still match.

cards.reteach: Think of Maya's house. Whether her equity is 70,000 or minus 70,000, house plus cash still equals mortgage plus her share. Balancing is automatic. Whether the share is big, small or negative is the interesting part, and that comes later.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A balance sheet lists what a company owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners. **Owns always equals owes plus owners' share**, because the owners' share is just the gap between the first two.
cards.simpler: A balance sheet lists three things. What a company owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners. **Owns always equals owes plus owners' share**, because the owners' share is just the gap between the first two. Think of a house with a mortgage: the house is worth what the bank is owed plus what the family really has.

cards.body: Tonight, search the name of any company you like plus "annual report balance sheet". Find the three totals and check that assets equal liabilities plus equity. Two minutes, and you have read your first one.
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick any company you like. Search its name along with the words annual report balance sheet. Find the three totals: what it owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners. Check that **owns equals owes plus owners' share**. It takes about two minutes, and then you have read your first real balance sheet.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now take any balance sheet, find the three totals, and show that what it owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to the owners.
